name: Choosing a Data Structure
intent: Pick a data structure by the operations the program actually does most (lookup, insert, range, smallest), by counting the steps each structure needs for that mix, and know what a step count leaves out.
scenario: A service keeps 1,000 records and starts with an unsorted array because it is the easiest. Lookups make up most of the traffic, so a hash map cuts them from 500,510 steps to 2,010. Later the same data feeds a report that asks for every record in a range, and the hash map, which keeps no order, now needs 1,505,550 steps for a report of 500 ranges, where a sorted array or a balanced tree needs about 10,000 to 11,000. A log writer that inserts all day is slow on the sorted array, which has to shift elements for each insert, and a job queue wants the smallest item over and over, which is what a heap is for.
problem: Every structure is fast at something and slow at something else, and the textbook table of Big O costs does not say which one your program needs. A hash map has the cheapest lookup and the worst range query. A sorted array has cheap range queries and expensive inserts. A heap finds its smallest item at once and cannot find anything else. Choosing by habit (a list for everything, or a hash map for everything) works until the workload changes, and then the cost shows up as latency. The way out is to write down the operations and how often each happens, count the steps for each candidate, and then remember that a count is not time: pointer-chasing structures such as linked lists and trees typically cost more per step than arrays on real hardware, so for small data and scan-heavy work the plain array often wins.

howItWorks.title: List the operations and their mix
howItWorks.text: Write down what the program does: how many lookups by key, inserts, range queries (all keys between two bounds) and reads of the smallest key, and how big the data is. A lookup-heavy cache, an append-only log, a report over date ranges and a job queue are four different workloads, and the same data structure is not the best for all of them.

howItWorks.title: Know what each structure is good at
howItWorks.text: An unsorted array or a linked list inserts in one step and finds anything only by scanning all items. A sorted array finds an item by halving the range and answers range and smallest queries cheaply, but every insert shifts the items after it. A hash map finds an item in a few steps and keeps no order, so a range or smallest query has to look at everything. A balanced tree keeps order and does lookup, insert, range and smallest in a number of steps that grows with the logarithm of the size. A binary heap inserts cheaply and always knows its smallest item, and has no way to find any other.

howItWorks.title: Count the steps for your mix
howItWorks.text: Multiply each operation's step count by how often it happens and add them up. With 1,000 items, a lookup-heavy mix (1,000 lookups, 10 inserts) costs 2,010 steps on a hash map and 500,510 on an unsorted array, and a report of 500 range queries (plus 20 lookups and 5 inserts) costs 10,141 on a balanced tree and 1,505,550 on a hash map. The winner changes with the mix, and a structure that is cheapest for few single operations, such as the balanced tree, can still win a mixed workload because it is never terrible.

howItWorks.title: Check what the count leaves out
howItWorks.text: A step is not a nanosecond. Arrays store items next to each other, so scanning one is typically fast per item because the processor reads ahead and caches it. Linked lists and trees follow pointers to scattered memory, which is typically slower per step. A hash map has the cost of computing the hash and of resizing, and a sorted array moves its items with one bulk copy, cheaper per item than the count suggests. For small data, a plain array scan frequently beats a cleverer structure, and only a measurement settles it.

howItWorks.title: Choose, then measure and revisit
howItWorks.text: Pick the structure that fits the mix and the size, hide it behind a small interface so it can be swapped, and measure with realistic data. Workloads drift: a lookup-only cache grows a reporting feature, and the structure that was right for the first month is wrong for the next. Counting steps for the new mix takes minutes and shows when it is time to change.

pros: Counting steps for the real operation mix picks the structure with evidence, not habit
A structure matched to the mix can cut the steps by orders of magnitude
Hiding the structure behind an interface makes it cheap to change when the workload changes
Balanced trees and sorted arrays serve several kinds of query, so they rarely fail badly
cons: Step counts ignore memory layout, caching and constant factors, which can reverse the order for small data
The operation mix has to be known or measured, and it changes over time
More specialised structures (heaps, trees) are more code and more places for bugs than a plain array
A structure that is best for one operation is often the worst for another
whenToUse: A hot path does one kind of operation far more than others, such as lookups, ordered scans or taking the smallest item
Data size is large enough that a scan is visibly slow, or is expected to grow
A profile shows time spent in a collection operation
whenNotToUse: Small collections, where a plain array scan is typically fast enough and the simplest code wins
Code that is not on a hot path, where the difference will never be noticed
Before measuring: guessing a clever structure for a workload you have not looked at
pitfalls: Using a hash map for everything, then needing a range query or sorted output, which it cannot give without visiting all items
Keeping a sorted array under heavy inserts: each insert shifts the later items
Using a heap to search for an item: it only knows its smallest, so any other lookup is a full scan
Choosing a linked list for cheap inserts and then scanning it: pointer-chasing is typically slow per step
Reading Big O as time: two structures with the same growth can differ by a large constant, and arrays are often faster than the count suggests
Picking the structure for today's mix and never counting again, while the workload shifts to ranges or ordered output
Forgetting that the cost table assumes a good hash function and balanced shape: skewed input can break both

roles.label: Workload
roles.description: The mix of operations the program performs.

roles.label: Hash map
roles.description: Finds a key in a few steps and keeps no order.

roles.label: Sorted array
roles.description: Searches by halving, answers ranges, pays on insert.

roles.label: Balanced tree
roles.description: Keeps order with logarithmic steps for most operations.

roles.label: Binary heap
roles.description: Always knows its smallest item, and little else.

quiz.question: A service needs to return every record whose timestamp is between two given values, many times a second. Which structure is a poor fit?
options: A hash map keyed by timestamp.
A sorted array with binary search for the lower bound.
quiz.explanation: A hash map keeps no order, so a range query has to visit every bucket and every item: 1,505,550 steps for a report of 500 ranges on 1,000 items against about 10,000 to 11,000 for a tree or sorted array.

quiz.question: A job queue inserts 500 jobs and reads (peeks at) the smallest one 500 times, on 1,000 items. Which structure fits best, and why?
options: A sorted array, because the smallest item is always first.
A hash map, because lookups cost only a few steps.
A linked list, because inserting at the head costs one step.
A binary heap, because it inserts in a few steps and reads its smallest at once.
quiz.explanation: The heap needs about 1,875 steps for this mix. The sorted array reads the smallest at once but pays to shift items on every insert, about 307,586 steps, and the hash map and list must scan to find the smallest. The model counts reads, not removals: removing the smallest would add one or two steps per level (about 10 levels here) to each removal for the heap and the tree.

quiz.question: A step count says a balanced tree needs fewer steps than a sorted array for a small collection, but a benchmark shows the array is faster. What is the most likely reason?
options: The count is wrong, because trees never need fewer steps.
The tree has a bug that makes it slow.
Arrays are stored contiguously, so each step is cheap, while following tree pointers costs more per step.
Benchmarks cannot be trusted for small data.
quiz.explanation: A step count treats every step as equal. Contiguous memory is typically read ahead and cached, so an array step is often cheaper than a pointer step. That is why small collections and scan-heavy work often favour arrays.
